title: The Shop Window Bride
premise: A display mannequin asks the player to stop a wedding scheduled in 1912.
pressure: A mannequin in a Ferndale shop window begs you to stop a wedding scheduled for 1912. A modern bus ticket lies under her veil. The shopkeeper says the display has never moved and asks you not to touch the dress.
investigate: Check the ceremony record before deciding the mannequin knows a real name
success: The archive contains a canceled ceremony, not a tragedy. Both people chose to leave town together. The mannequin looks faintly pleased and declines to explain why.
failure: The clock in the display coughs and the names vanish from the card. You retain the bus ticket and the good sense not to accuse anyone's ancestors.
help: Ask the shopkeeper about the display and protect the family's privacy
helpOutcome: The shopkeeper changes the display with the family's permission. A visitor recognizes a photograph and asks to keep the story private.

title: The Cow Who Owns the Theater
premise: An elegantly dressed cow has inherited a very specific deed.
pressure: A cow in a velvet coat has inherited a Ferndale theater. The board declares that a hoofprint cannot authorize the payroll. Rain drips through the orchestra pit roof onto a violinist's empty chair. 'I can either rehearse or hold a bucket,' the stage manager says. The cow snorts at the board's proposed renovation budget, which is mostly new curtains for the donor lounge.
investigate: Read the deed beside the company's books, not just the animal's costume
success: The deed is ordinary apart from a signature dated fifty years ahead. The accounts are worse: the balcony needs repair and the crew has not been paid. The cow points its nose at the wage column until a board member stops talking about destiny and starts asking for figures. You verify the discrepancy, not the animal's legal standing.
failure: Rain smears the last page of the deed and the board calls your uncertainty proof that the cow cannot inherit. A clerk confirms the family owned the building, not who speaks for the new beneficiary. The stage manager asks whether you can help pay tonight's crew instead of winning tomorrow's court case.
help: Help the company rehearse while its patron and workers negotiate
helpOutcome: You help the company stage a smaller show while the board and crew negotiate a wage advance. The cow takes the cheap seat near the orchestra pit so the money goes to repairs. 'Best patron we've ever had,' a violinist says. 'Though she did eat the second-act program.'

title: Victorian House of Cards
premise: A tourist attraction's floor plan is rearranged by drawing cards.
pressure: A Victorian tour house rearranges its rooms whenever someone draws from a battered deck. The guide is stuck on a landing between two staircases and one guest keeps filming instead of listening to her directions. A fire exit sign now points toward a linen closet.
investigate: Mark the stair positions and compare them with the posted escape plan
success: The cards reproduce three room layouts in a repeatable order. The guide preserves the sequence for inspectors while you locate an actual ground-floor exit.
failure: The house reshuffles when you mark the final landing. You still record which doorway leads outside and which one merely promises to.
help: Help the guide escort everyone out before trying another card
helpOutcome: All guests reach the garden and the guide gets a headcount. The house deals itself a consolation card marked TRY AGAIN TOMORROW.

title: The Pie Contest with a Second Jury
premise: An unseen panel awards prizes based on regrets, not flavor.
pressure: An invisible jury has joined the Ferndale pie contest. It scores each baker's most intimate regret rather than the crust, and now insists that a thirteen-year-old competitor describe something she has never told her family. 'My pie has blackberries,' she says. 'That's all I entered.' The fair organizer is afraid to disqualify judges nobody can see, because half the crowd has started cheering for the supernatural round.
investigate: Ask the invisible judges to reveal their rules and who authorized them
success: You uncover the second jury's scorecards, already dated for next year's contest. An organizer admits she let the strange judges take a table because they promised publicity. The young baker asks whether she can withdraw her statement without withdrawing her pie. You give the organizer the rules and make her answer in front of the entrants. The invisible jury protests that secrets add flavor.
failure: A pie tin rings like a dinner gong, and the invisible jury departs with its scorecards. You cannot prove which baker was pressured into revealing what. The organizer proposes keeping the mysterious rankings because people enjoyed the show. The thirteen-year-old asks her to explain why a grown-up's entertainment should count more than a child's privacy. The room gets very quiet.
help: Let the bakers withdraw personal stories while keeping their pies in the contest
helpOutcome: You ask the bakers, not the audience, which contest they actually entered. They agree to a second tasting using the announced rules, with private stories kept private. The invisible jury calls this censorship from somewhere under the table. The youngest competitor wins a ribbon for a crust that survives the trip home and tells everyone absolutely nothing about her diary.

title: Parade Float of Future Regrets
premise: A float features the player's decisions with embarrassing accuracy.
pressure: A parade float features a miniature of your weekend, including a particularly embarrassing decision you have yet to make. A teenage maker is being accused of spying on you, although she built the set from donated scraps and has never met you.
investigate: Ask the maker how she designed the tableau and compare its details with your notes
success: She shows a sketch dated before the event it depicts. You keep the drawing with her permission, not as proof that she knows your mind.
failure: A gust carries off the miniature before anyone can agree what it showed. The maker remembers the costume seam you had noticed yourself.
help: Defend the maker from accusations and help repair the float
helpOutcome: The parade continues and the maker gets credit for her work. Your miniature bows to the crowd without waiting for your permission.

title: The River Lodge Has No Exit
premise: A conference room exits into every other conference room at once.
pressure: At a Fortuna lodge, every conference-room door opens into the same conference room. A server carrying cold coffee has passed the same EXIT sign six times, and the hotel manager keeps insisting the floor plan has always been adequate.
investigate: Check the posted evacuation plan against the doors and the headcount
success: Behind one door is a meeting about river restoration dated fifteen years from now. You note what the sign says and return to the present guests, who have more immediate questions.
failure: The corridor folds back to the lobby while your pencil is still drawing it. A keycard for an unbuilt room remains in your pocket, but everybody can account for where they are.
help: Stop the meeting and guide everyone toward one confirmed exit together
helpOutcome: The staff lead the guests out by the service hall and count them twice. The manager agrees to replace the fire plan before advertising a conference on miracles.

title: An Extremely Civilized Were-Bear
premise: A genial local asks for help with noise complaints during full moons.
pressure: A courteous were-bear has brought noise-complaint letters from three neighbors to a hearing. One asks for quiet; another likes the monthly roar because it tells her the storm is turning; the third wants a soundproof fence. None wants a supernatural wildlife trial.
investigate: Compare the complaint times with the sound readings and the calendar
success: A faulty culvert amplifies the roar toward one house. The county can inspect it without deciding whether anyone is a were-bear.
failure: The recording captures only wind. The neighbors agree on when the loudest night occurred and submit signed statements instead.
help: Help the neighbors negotiate a trial quiet period and safe meeting place
helpOutcome: They arrange a test and exchange contact numbers. The were-bear thanks the clerk, then nearly eats the microphone cover by mistake.

title: The Hardware Store Crop Circle
premise: A perfect circle appears in the aisle of extension cords.
pressure: A perfect crop circle has appeared in a hardware store's extension-cord aisle. The hum makes the checkout terminal skip numbers, and the owner is blaming students. A cashier is standing beside a hot cable nobody should touch.
investigate: Trace the power circuit and check the cord labels without entering the circle
success: The humming cords carry tomorrow's inventory stickers. You photograph the labels after the owner isolates the power.
failure: The breaker trips before you get a clean reading. A scorch mark identifies the outlet that needs inspection.
help: Move shoppers clear and help the owner shut down the unsafe display
helpOutcome: No one gets shocked and the owner stops accusing students. The cords quietly arrange themselves into a complaint about store hours.

title: The Lost Receipt of Destiny
premise: A cashier recognizes a receipt for an object that has not been invented.
pressure: At a Fortuna counter, a cashier hands you a receipt for an invention that won't exist for years. It names an unborn customer and a serial number from tomorrow's shipment. The manager thinks the cashier invented the transaction to cover a register shortage.
investigate: Compare the printed part numbers and the till audit before anyone assigns blame
success: The parts describe an achievable habitat sensor, but none are missing from inventory. The manager records the anomaly and clears the cashier's till.
failure: The thermal paper fades before the device name can be read. The serial prefix and till total survive in the cashier's notebook.
help: Help the cashier document the glitch and complete a fair reconciliation
helpOutcome: The books balance and no wages are withheld. The receipt goes in a labeled envelope; it is the least convenient form of future technology.

title: The Eel River Forecast Desk
premise: A volunteer weather station forecasts emotional conditions alongside rainfall.
pressure: The Eel River volunteer forecast station predicts rainfall and emotional weather. Tomorrow's river stage is printed next to APOLOGY, and a resident wants to know whether the machine is publicly announcing her private argument. The storm itself is real.
investigate: Compare the gauge history with the station's printed emotional forecasts
success: The rain numbers match regional readings; the apology field has no measurement behind it. You keep the useful flood advisory and reject the gossip.
failure: The paper jams before the flood crest time prints. A volunteer can still read the gauge directly and phone a confirmed level upstream.
help: Help volunteers post a clear weather warning without naming private residents
helpOutcome: The flood notice reaches the river users. Someone writes PLEASE APOLOGIZE IN PERSON beneath the broken emotional forecast printer.

title: The Tree with a Reception Desk
premise: A hollow redwood hosts a receptionist for the forest's impossible visitors.
pressure: An enormous redwood has acquired a tiny reception desk, complete with number tickets and a brass bell. The receptionist welcomes visitors from several centuries but asks every tourist to stay on the public path. A developer wants to sell guided access to the tree's hollow.
investigate: Request permission to read the visitor ledger without copying private names
success: The ledger lists a park ranger from a future year, arriving to inspect an unbuilt path. The receptionist lets you copy the path sketch, with its uncertainties left intact.
failure: The ledger politely closes on your hand when you ask for a name. You leave with a public trail map and a reminder that evidence is not the same as permission.
help: Support a visitor plan that protects the grove and keeps ordinary hikers welcome
helpOutcome: The queue moves onto the marked trail, the developer takes down the sales sign, and the receptionist resumes stamping tickets for visitors who know which century they are in.

title: The Giant's Smaller Older Brother
premise: An enormous silhouette insists the real giant is just off-trail.
pressure: An enormous silhouette points beyond the redwoods and insists its older brother is smaller. Each witness describes a different height, while a tour operator starts leading paying visitors onto a closed restoration trail.
investigate: Compare shadow angles and witnesses from the public path
success: The silhouette's edges track a patch of moving fog, but a tiny second set of footprints ends at the fence. You record both without trespassing.
failure: The shadows overlap before a scale can be measured. A park visitor shares a photo with the trail boundary clearly visible.
help: Ask the operator to keep visitors on the open path and give the restoration crew room
helpOutcome: The crowd moves back and the seedlings remain undisturbed. The smaller older brother declines to be photographed, a wise family policy.

title: A Roadside Attraction for Ghost Cars
premise: Invisible tourists keep buying tickets to an abandoned exhibit.
pressure: Invisible tourists queue in perfect order at an abandoned roadside attraction on the Avenue of the Giants. They pay with folded blank paper. The neighboring shopkeeper is worried about traffic on a narrow shoulder, and somebody has reopened a crumbling ticket booth without asking.
investigate: Read the guestbook and inspect the receipts without stepping into traffic
success: Every signature names tomorrow's date and a bridge dismantled years ago. The paper feels new. The shopkeeper can confirm the booth was locked yesterday.
failure: A gust tears the page away before you copy all the names. An empty ticket machine prints a fresh stub and deposits it neatly beside your shoe.
help: Turn the unsafe turnout into a free, marked place to pause and find directions
helpOutcome: The shopkeeper lends a water jug and volunteers place clear warning cones. Visible and invisible travelers take turns without making the road an exhibit.

title: The Redwood Rings of Tomorrow
premise: A fallen log records two more summers than have occurred.
pressure: A fallen redwood has two extra rings, one for each summer nobody remembers. A contractor wants to carve out a slice and sell it as proof of prophecy before the park's volunteer sawyer can document it.
investigate: Count the rings with the sawyer and compare growth bands without removing wood
success: The extra bands correspond to a drought nobody has recorded. The park receives photographs and a marked measurement, not a souvenir.
failure: A knot disrupts your count and your tally contradicts the sawyer's. The contractor photographs the disagreement and announces an exclusive prophecy. The sawyer pins both unverified tallies to the volunteer noticeboard. You have made a record of what nobody knows yet, which does not sell nearly as well.
help: Help the volunteers protect the log from unauthorized cutting
helpOutcome: The contractor backs off and the trail crew posts a clear explanation. The log gets to keep its extra summers.

title: The Family Portrait in the Bark
premise: A tree's scars resemble a family the player has just met.
pressure: In the bark of a redwood, a scar resembles a family you spoke with earlier, including a child they never mentioned. The likeness shifts when the canopy moves. A stranger with a camera wants to send it to the family before asking whether they want it.
investigate: Sketch the bark from the boardwalk at two different angles
success: A new figure appears in the shadow of the sketch, carrying a strange pruning tool. You label what changed and avoid naming a relative who may not exist.
failure: The sun moves and the faces dissolve into an ordinary scar. You keep both sketches, marked with their positions, rather than declaring the forest a family historian.
help: Ask the family whether they want to hear about the resemblance before showing images
helpOutcome: The family chooses to see the sketches privately and asks you not to post them. The tree retains its shape, and the family retains the right to tell its own story.

title: The Backwoods Crop that Talks Back
premise: A remote garden's sentient scarecrow wants employment protections.
pressure: A scarecrow on an Eel River farm requests dry straw and Sunday off. Its owner calls it equipment at payroll and a colleague whenever the roof leaks. 'I've worked sixty-three consecutive dawns,' the scarecrow says, opening a notebook with twine fingers. The grower admits there is nobody to take the shift. The scarecrow answers, 'That sounds like a management problem with a hat.'
investigate: Compare the farm's written agreements with what the scarecrow has actually done
success: The labor log lists the scarecrow as both an asset and the signer of supply orders. The owner says it was easier than filling out the paperwork. You record the contradiction and show both of them the entries. The scarecrow takes the notebook back: 'You can verify my work. You can't decide what my Sunday means.'
failure: Rain melts the ink on the owner's contract, including the paragraph you came to verify. The scarecrow produces its own careful shift notes, but they do not settle who promised what. The grower accuses it of keeping a secret ledger; the scarecrow replies that nobody asked until it requested a day off.
help: Help negotiate safe work limits and rest while the owner sorts out the records
helpOutcome: You help line up a paid relief shift so the scarecrow can spend Sunday beneath a newly patched roof. The grower worries aloud about the budget. The scarecrow starts its first break by asking whether it is allowed to do nothing. 'It's harder than it looks,' the replacement says, settling into the watch.

title: The Moonshine of Mixed Timelines
premise: A homebrewed drink makes two contradictory memories equally convincing.
pressure: Two neighbors share a homebrew recipe and remember opposite versions of the same harvest. Neither recollection proves anything about the other's honesty. Their argument has reached the point where one is about to publish accusations on the community board.
investigate: Compare dates and crop records while making no claims about what the drink causes
success: Both notebooks are internally consistent but the harvest receipts differ. You document the discrepancy and leave the neighbors free to revise their stories.
failure: The old receipt is illegible and the recipe offers no answer. Each neighbor can still name a third witness who might remember the day.
help: Help them postpone the public accusation and agree on one checkable question
helpOutcome: They set down the bottles and call the packing crew. Dinner remains awkward, but nobody's reputation is decided by an argument about memories.

title: The Farmer's Unmarked Helicopter
premise: A low-flying craft is piloted by something that understands zoning rules.
pressure: An unmarked helicopter keeps tracing the garden boundary with unnatural precision. The pilot knows obscure zoning clauses; the grower fears somebody is filming private workers and the neighbors fear the craft will strike a power line.
investigate: Map the aircraft's path against public zoning boundaries from safe ground
success: The route follows a proposed parcel change not yet on the public agenda. You note the filing number and refer the low flight to aviation authorities.
failure: The craft vanishes into fog before you can read a marking. A neighbor captured its altitude against the line of a barn roof.
help: Help workers move out of the landing area and document the safety concern
helpOutcome: The grower closes the field briefly, everyone gets indoors and the helicopter leaves. The zoning complaint is filed without revealing anyone's private plants.

title: The River Stone Adoption Agency
premise: A family insists their pet rock is the rightful heir to a ranch.
pressure: An Eel River family arrives at the county clerk's desk with a will naming a river stone as heir to a ranch. The clerk has handled disputes over cattle and fences, but not probate involving an object that cannot sign. Two relatives are already arguing over the riverbank.
investigate: Examine the will and the stone's marks with the family and clerk present
success: A line of scratches records flood levels that match old field notes and suggest one vulnerable pasture. The stone may be an odd heir, but the risk is practical and needs a plan.
failure: The envelope's ink smears before you can read the signature. The relatives still remember the stone's history and the clerk offers a proper way to preserve their testimony.
help: Help the heirs agree on access and bank protection while probate is reviewed
helpOutcome: The family keeps the stone on the mantel and drafts a shared-use agreement for the riverbank. Nobody wins the ranch by throwing its heir.

title: A Small Pagan Book Club
premise: A fictional occult reading group accidentally summons its own literary critic.
pressure: A small fictional occult book club has summoned a literary critic by reading a bad ending aloud. The apparition calls every character a symbol and demands a rewrite before letting the members go home. The librarian wants the group to stop insulting her volunteers.
investigate: Ask the critic to cite the text rather than pass judgment on the readers
success: The apparition identifies a missing scene instead of an allegedly deficient person. The author can revise it later, if they choose.
failure: The critic speaks entirely in footnotes and everyone loses the thread. A book-club member copies the one useful question onto a bookmark.
help: Help the club close the meeting on time and let each reader keep their interpretation
helpOutcome: They return the chairs and make a potluck date. The critic gets a library card, probationary, and a very long list of overdue opinions.
